items.title: Bay of Bengal marine outlook: moderate swell on East Coast corridor
items.summary: Operational outlook flags moderate wave and residual monsoon exposure for Odisha–Andhra shipping lanes; berth windows should retain weather margin.

items.title: Dry-bulk freight market remains sensitive to Capesize demand
items.summary: Capesize-led Pacific activity is keeping the dry-bulk curve firm; charterers with 30–60 day cover should compare spot exposure with consecutive-voyage cover.

items.title: Indian Ocean vessel availability remains a key scheduling variable
items.summary: Positioning and ballast distance can materially change the effective cost of a fixture, particularly for multi-voyage programmes.

items.title: Monsoon residual risk can affect lighterage and berth windows
items.summary: East Coast discharge plans should include queue and weather buffers rather than relying on sailing time alone.

items.title: Route economics diverge by vessel class and trade lane
items.summary: Australia, Indonesia, Mozambique, Brazil and US Gulf trades show different freight sensitivities; class-specific curves are used by the chartering layer.

items.title: Port turnaround remains a material part of effective voyage time
items.summary: Handling capacity, berth availability and queue days are included alongside sea passage and inland delivery in FreightOne route scoring.

items.title: Long-haul cargoes carry higher bunker and market exposure
items.summary: Brazil and US Gulf routes have greater voyage duration, making bunker and freight-rate assumptions more important in total landed-cost comparisons.

items.title: Marine risk should be checked before fixing narrow laycans
items.summary: When the deadline is tight, FreightOne prioritises feasible ETA over waiting for a projected soft-rate window.
